overview: The humble LED is usually the very first component anyone wires up, and for good reason: it's simple, forgiving to experiment with, and visually confirms that a circuit works. It only conducts current in one direction (unlike a resistor), so it must be wired the correct way around — the longer lead is positive (anode), the shorter lead (often next to a flat edge on the plastic case) is negative (cathode) — and it always needs a current-limiting resistor in series, since an LED offers almost no resistance of its own and will draw damaging (or fatal-to-the-LED) current directly off a voltage source otherwise.
simpleSummary: A small light that turns on when current flows through it — usually the very first part anyone wires up.

specifications.polarity: Polarized — anode (+, longer lead) and cathode (-, shorter lead, flat edge on case)
specifications.package: Common sizes: 3mm, 5mm through-hole; various SMD sizes

pinMap.name: Anode (+)
pinMap.function: Positive terminal — the longer lead on a new LED.
pinMap.voltageRange: Forward voltage drop (~1.8-3.4V depending on color)
pinMap.currentLimit: ~15-20 mA (needs a series resistor to enforce this)
pinMap.gotcha: Never wire an LED directly across a voltage source without a current-limiting resistor in series — it will draw far more current than rated and burn out almost immediately.

pinMap.name: Cathode (-)
pinMap.function: Negative terminal — the shorter lead, next to a flat edge on the LED's plastic case.
pinMap.gotcha: Wired backwards, an LED simply won't light (it doesn't burn out from reverse voltage within its rated limits) — if an LED does nothing, check polarity before assuming it's broken.

useCases.title: Status indicator
useCases.scenario: The classic first project — light an LED to confirm a pin can be driven HIGH/LOW.

useCases.title: Simple visual feedback
useCases.scenario: Indicate a sensor threshold being crossed, a mode change, or an error condition.

useCases.title: PWM-dimmed mood lighting
useCases.scenario: Use analogWrite/PWM to vary brightness smoothly rather than simple on/off.
